messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David has not felt safe in four years, not since the IED turned a dusty road in Kandahar into a storm of noise and heat. He had been arguing with his sergeant, a trivial disagreement about the patrol route, when the world dissolved. The memory rarely comes as a clear narrative. Instead, it is a sensory assault. The most persistent element is the taste—a gritty, metallic mix of dust and blood that can fill his mouth without warning, as vivid as if the explosion had happened moments ago. When this happens, the raw terror of that day floods him, so overwhelming he has to brace himself against a wall or grip the edge of his desk until it subsides. Other times, the events replay with a chilling detachment; he can see the bodies and the wreckage with perfect clarity but feels nothing, as if watching a film about a stranger. Because the memory could ambush him with such visceral force or with such unnerving detachment, he began to perceive threats in otherwise mundane interactions, his mind constantly searching for anything—a tone of voice, a sudden movement—that might signal a repeat of the initial conflict before the blast.

This fragmented, intrusive past dictates the terms of his present life as a tax consultant. Triggers are everywhere, ambushing him in the sterile quiet of his office. A tense conversation with a client about an audit, with its undercurrent of confrontation, is enough to bring back the taste of blood and the suffocating panic. This visceral recall immediately activates his perceived need for escape. He will find his eyes darting to the nearest exit, his mind automatically plotting the quickest route out of the building, a constant, humming state of threat assessment that leaves him exhausted. This background hum of danger makes ordinary cues feel like active threats, turning the normal pressures of his work into a landscape of potential ambushes. In the aftermath of such an episode, he will retreat into himself for days, refusing to discuss the client meeting or anything that touches upon conflict, a strategy of avoidance he believes is necessary for survival.

The strategies he uses to manage the terror have, over time, become prisons. His wife, Sarah, no longer reaches for his hand. Early in their reunion, she tried, but any unexpected touch would cause him to flinch violently, his body reacting with an animal panic that he couldn't control. Now, he preemptively avoids all physical contact, creating a painful distance between them. This avoidance has made him even more sensitive, so that the mere possibility of being touched feels like a threat in itself. He has also learned to smother any flicker of happiness. A moment of genuine laughter with a colleague or a feeling of pride in his work is immediately pushed away, squashed by the conviction that letting his guard down, even for a second, is an invitation for disaster.

These self-protective measures create a vicious, self-sustaining loop. The more he avoids talking about the trauma, the more the memories ambush him, often in their most detached and unnerving form. The silence he cultivates by pushing others away has become its own source of terror; a quiet house no longer feels peaceful but pregnant with menace, the same ringing stillness that followed the explosion. In these charged silences, his threat system is on high alert, which in turn makes it more likely that a fragment of memory will surface. The memory then reinforces his belief that the world is unsafe, deepening his reliance on the very avoidance strategies that are isolating him and sensitising him to new triggers. A simple head cold now feels catastrophic, the physical discomfort immediately connecting in his mind to the feeling of his own wounds after the blast, triggering a fresh wave of intrusive sensory fragments.

David came to therapy because Sarah told him she felt like she was living with a ghost. The man she loved had been replaced by a perimeter of defenses she could no longer breach. He sat rigidly in the chair, his hands clenched, admitting that he was losing everything he had fought to come home to. His greatest fear is that the damage is permanent, that the man he was is gone for good. His hope, whispered with a profound sense of shame, is simply to be able to hold his wife’s hand again without feeling like he is about to die.
